title: AQA GCSE Physics · Particle Model of Matter

rounds.name: Changes of state and the particle model

items.stem: Which of these is the definition of the density of a material?

options.text: The volume the sample fills divided by its own mass.
The mass of the sample multiplied by the volume.
The mass of the sample divided by its volume.
The total mass the sample happens to have.

items.why: This is the definition the specification gives: density = mass / volume.

items.stem: In the equation ρ = m/V, what do the symbols m and V stand for?

options.text: m stands for mass and V stands for volume.
m stands for metres and V stands for volume.
m stands for mass and V is the speed it moves.
m stands for the weight and V for the volume.

items.why: These are the quantities the specification lists for this equation: mass, m, in kilograms and volume, V, in metres cubed.

items.stem: Which unit does the specification use for density?

options.text: kilograms times metres cubed, kg m³
kilograms per metre squared, kg/m²
kilograms per metre cubed, written kg/m³
grams per centimetre cubed, g/cm³

items.why: The specification gives density, ρ, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m^3, which follows from dividing a mass in kg by a volume in m^3.

items.stem: A cube of steel has sides of 0.10 m and a mass of 7.8 kg. What is its density?

options.text: 7800 kg/m³
780 kg/m³
78 kg/m³

items.stem: A liquid has a density of 800 kg/m³. What volume is occupied by 2.0 kg of the liquid?

options.text: 400 m³

items.why: Rearranging ρ = m/V gives V = m/ρ = 2.0 / 800 = 0.0025 m^3.

items.stem: Aluminium has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. What is this density in kg/m³?

options.text: 2.7 kg/m³
2700 kg/m³
27 kg/m³

items.why: One g/cm^3 is 1000 kg/m^3, so 2.7 g/cm^3 x 1000 = 2700 kg/m^3.

items.stem: A rectangular block measures 0.30 m by 0.20 m by 0.10 m. What is its volume?

options.text: 0.6 m³
6 m³

items.why: Volume of a cuboid = length x width x height = 0.30 x 0.20 x 0.10 = 0.006 m^3.

items.stem: A balance shows the mass of a block as 250 g. Which value should be used for m to obtain a density in kg/m³?

options.text: 250 000 kg, the reading multiplied by 1000
250 kg, the balance reading itself
2.5 N, the weight the balance is showing
0.25 kg, the reading divided by 1000

items.why: The equation needs mass in kilograms, and 250 g is 250 / 1000 = 0.25 kg.

items.stem: A solid aluminium bar is cut exactly in half. What is the density of each half?

options.text: Half the original value, since each piece has half the mass.
A quarter of the original value, since mass times volume is used.
A little lower, since each half now weighs less.
The same as the whole bar, because mass and volume both halve.

items.why: Density is a property of the material. Halving the mass and the volume together leaves the ratio unchanged.

items.stem: Which statement describes the arrangement of particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas?

options.text: Solid: regular and touching; liquid: evenly spaced out; gas: far apart.
Solid: small particles; liquid: larger ones; gas: the largest of all.
Solid: regular with wide gaps; liquid: random and touching; gas: random.
Solid: regular and touching; liquid: random but touching; gas: random and far apart.

items.why: This matches the particle model: solids and liquids both have particles in contact, and only the gas has widely separated particles.

items.stem: A student is drawing simple particle diagrams. Which drawing models a liquid correctly?

options.text: Circles of one size in a neat grid, evenly spaced.
Circles of one size touching, with no pattern.
Circles drawn larger than those in the solid diagram.
Circles spread far apart and scattered across the box.

items.why: In a liquid the particles are still in contact, as in a solid, but the arrangement is random so they can slide past one another.

items.stem: Why is the density of steam so much lower than the density of liquid water?

options.text: Its molecules are much further apart, so that mass fills more space.
Its molecules are lighter and smaller than those in the liquid water, too.
Some of the water's mass is destroyed when the liquid is boiled away.
Each molecule swells up as it is heated, so the steam weighs less.

items.why: The particle model explains density differences through spacing: the molecules are unchanged, but each cubic metre of steam holds far fewer of them.

items.stem: Ice floats on liquid water. What does this show about ice, and why?

options.text: It is less dense, because its molecules are held slightly further apart.
It is denser, because the solid state of a substance is always the denser one.
It is lighter, because a little mass is lost as the water freezes.
It has smaller molecules than water, which is what makes it rise.

items.why: Water is unusual: freezing locks the molecules into an open arrangement, so the same mass occupies a larger volume and the density falls to about 920 kg/m^3.

items.stem: A student is finding the density of a rectangular metal block. Which measurements are needed?

options.text: The mass from a balance, and the length of one side from a ruler.
The mass from a balance, and the length, width and height from a ruler.
The mass from a balance, and the area of one face from a ruler.
The weight in newtons, and the three dimensions from a ruler.

items.why: For a regularly shaped object the specification expects the volume to come from its dimensions, so all three lengths are needed along with the mass.

items.stem: A measuring cylinder holds 50 cm³ of water. A stone is lowered in and the level rises to 128 cm³. What is the volume of the stone?

options.text: 178 cm³, the two cylinder readings added
128 cm³, the final reading on the cylinder
78 cm³, the rise in the water level
50 cm³, the water already in the cylinder

items.why: The volume of an irregular object is the volume of water it displaces, which is the final reading minus the starting reading: 128 - 50 = 78 cm^3.

items.stem: A student measures the density of cooking oil with a measuring cylinder on a balance. Which mass is divided by the volume of oil?

options.text: The mass of the measuring cylinder once the oil has been poured in.
The mass of cylinder and oil minus the mass of the empty cylinder.
The mass of the empty measuring cylinder before the oil is added.
The mass of the empty cylinder added to the mass of cylinder and oil.

items.why: Only the oil occupies the measured volume, so the mass of the glass must be subtracted before dividing.

items.stem: Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the diameter of a copper wire about 0.4 mm across?

options.text: Vernier callipers, since they read in mm too.
A millimetre rule, estimated by eye.
A micrometer, reading to 0.01 mm.
Any of them, since all read in mm.

items.why: The resolution needs to be small compared with 0.4 mm. A micrometer reading to 0.01 mm measures the diameter to about two per cent.

items.stem: A sealed container holds 200 g of ice. The container is left until all the ice has melted. What does the balance read now?

options.text: 200 g, because melting rearranges the particles but removes none.
Less than 200 g, because some of the ice gets used up as it melts.
More than 200 g, since liquid water is denser than solid ice.
100 g, since the water takes up far less room than the ice.

items.why: Mass is conserved in a change of state. The container is sealed, so nothing can enter or leave.

items.stem: Solid carbon dioxide sublimates in an open dish on a balance and the reading falls to zero. Has any mass been destroyed?

options.text: Yes, subliming uses the solid up, so that mass has gone for good now.
No, but gases weigh nothing at all, so the reading had to fall away.
Yes, because a gas is a new substance made out of that solid.
No, the gas has spread into the room and is not on the balance.

items.why: Sublimation is a change of state, so mass is conserved. The balance reads zero only because the carbon dioxide is no longer on the pan.

items.stem: Why is boiling water classed as a physical change rather than a chemical change?

options.text: Steam is a new substance, but a very easy one to turn back.
Physical changes are reversible and chemical changes are not.
Boiling can be undone, so it cannot be a chemical change.
The steam is still water; cooling gives the liquid back.

items.why: In a physical change no new substance is formed, and reversing the change recovers the original properties.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the internal energy of a system?

options.text: The energy stored inside the system by its own particles
The temperature the system reaches when it is heated
The heat that flowed in and is now held inside
The energy the system gives out to its surroundings

items.why: Energy is stored inside a system by the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up the system, and that store is called internal energy.

items.stem: Internal energy is the total of which two energy stores of the particles in a system?

options.text: The chemical energy and the thermal energy of all the particles
The kinetic energy and the potential energy of the particles
The kinetic energy of every one of the particles, only
The kinetic energy stored as the particles move about

items.why: Internal energy is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles that make up a system.

items.stem: Where does the potential energy part of a system's internal energy come from?

options.text: From the speeds at which the particles are moving about inside
From the height of the system above the floor of the laboratory
From the positions of particles and the forces between them
From the temperature the system has been raised to

items.why: Particles attract one another, so energy is stored in how they are arranged; that is the potential energy part.

items.stem: Heating a system increases the energy of the particles that make it up. Which pair of outcomes does the specification give for this?

options.text: It always raises the temperature of the system, without exception
It raises the temperature and it always changes state as well
It raises the pressure or else it produces a change of state
It raises the temperature or it produces a change of state

items.why: This is what the specification states: heating either raises the temperature of the system or produces a change of state.

items.stem: A beaker of ice at 0 °C is heated steadily by an immersion heater until all the ice has melted. What does the heating do during that time?

options.text: It raises the temperature of the ice steadily as it melts
It increases the energy stored and produces a change of state
The energy stored stays the same as the temperature holds steady
It has no effect until the ice reaches its melting point

items.why: The energy supplied increases the energy of the particles and produces the change of state from solid to liquid.

items.stem: When a substance is heated and its temperature increases, the size of that increase depends on which three things?

options.text: The volume, the type of material and the total time of heating
The mass, the final temperature and the energy supplied
The mass, the type of material and the energy input to it
The mass, the energy input and the type of container

items.why: These are the three factors the specification lists for the increase in temperature.

items.stem: 1 kg of water and 1 kg of cooking oil are each supplied with 20 000 J. The oil ends up much hotter than the water. Why?

options.text: Equal masses given equal energy must reach equal temperatures
The oil has a much higher specific heat capacity than water
The oil is thicker, so the heater warms it up quickly
Oil has a lower specific heat capacity than the water does

items.why: The increase in temperature depends on the type of material; oil needs less energy per kilogram per degree Celsius.

items.stem: Which word equation for the change in thermal energy is the one given in the specification?

options.text: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × the final temperature
change in thermal energy = mass × specific latent heat × the temperature change
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity ÷ the temperature change

items.why: This is the specification equation, written in symbols as ∆E = m c ∆θ.

items.stem: In the equation ∆E = m c ∆θ, what do the symbols c and ∆θ stand for?

options.text: c is the specific heat capacity and ∆θ is the final temperature
c is the specific latent heat and ∆θ is the temperature change
c is the specific heat capacity and ∆θ is the temperature change
c is the capacity of the container and ∆θ is a state change

items.why: In ∆E = m c ∆θ, c is specific heat capacity in J/kg °C and ∆θ is the temperature change in °C.

items.stem: In which of these situations does the equation ∆E = m c ∆θ apply?

options.text: While ice at 0 °C melts into water that is also at 0 °C
While water at 100 °C is boiling away steadily into steam
While water at 0 °C freezes solid inside a freezer
While the water in a kettle warms from 20 °C up to 90 °C

items.why: The temperature of the water is changing with no change of state, which is when ∆E = m c ∆θ applies.

items.stem: In ∆E = m c ∆θ, which units does the specification give for ∆E and for ∆θ?

options.text: ∆E is in joules, J, and ∆θ is in degrees Celsius, °C
∆E in joules per second, and ∆θ in degrees Celsius, °C
∆E in joules, and ∆θ in joules per kilogram, J/kg
∆E in joules, and ∆θ in J/kg °C

items.why: The specification gives change in thermal energy, ∆E, in joules, J, and temperature change, ∆θ, in degrees Celsius, °C.

items.stem: A student uses ∆E = m c ∆θ for a 250 g block of aluminium. What should be substituted for m?

options.text: 250, because that is the mass given in the question
0.25, because the mass must be in kilograms
2.50, because grams are converted by dividing by 100
250 000, since kilograms are the larger unit here

items.why: Mass, m, is in kilograms, so 250 g is divided by 1000 to give 0.25 kg.

items.stem: What are the units of specific heat capacity, and why does a temperature appear in them?

options.text: J/kg, because the value is quoted for one kilogram of substance
J/°C, because the value is quoted for one degree Celsius
J/kg °C, because the substance is heated for one whole minute
J/kg °C, because the value fixes one kilogram and a one degree rise

items.why: Specific heat capacity, c, is in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C, matching its definition.

items.stem: Which statement is the specification definition of the specific heat capacity of a substance?

options.text: The energy required to raise one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius
The energy required to raise the whole of the sample by one degree Celsius
The energy required to change the state of one kilogram of it
The energy stored by one kilogram of it at a given temperature

items.why: This is the definition: the energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.

items.stem: Blocks P and Q have the same mass. P has the higher specific heat capacity. The same energy is supplied to each block. What happens?

options.text: P has the greater temperature rise, because its capacity is larger
Q has the greater temperature rise, needing less energy per °C
Both rise by the same amount, since the energy supplied is equal
Q must change state first, because its capacity is smaller

items.why: Q needs fewer joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, so the same energy raises its temperature more.

items.stem: 10 500 J are supplied to 0.50 kg of water, which does not boil. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. What is the temperature change?
10 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 50 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. What is the change in thermal energy?
What is meant by the latent heat of a substance?

options.text: The energy stored by a substance once it has melted
The energy that is needed for a substance to change state
The energy needed to raise a substance by one degree
The energy lost by a substance while its temperature is constant

items.why: The specification calls the energy needed for a substance to change state its latent heat.

items.stem: Steam is produced steadily from boiling water at 100 °C. What happens to the energy that is supplied?

options.text: It raises the temperature of the water past 100 °C
It is stored in the heater until the boiling has finished
It changes the energy stored but not the temperature
It leaves the water's own internal energy unchanged

items.why: During a change of state the energy supplied changes the internal energy of the substance, not its temperature.

items.stem: Which energy store of the particles increases while a solid melts at constant temperature?

options.text: Their kinetic energy, because the particles must be moving faster
Their thermal energy, as heat flows into the solid and is stored
Neither store, because the temperature is not changing at all
Their potential energy, as the particles are pulled apart

items.why: The energy supplied separates the particles against the forces between them, raising their potential energy store.

items.stem: Which statement is the specification definition of the specific latent heat of a substance?

options.text: The energy needed to change the state of a whole sample of it
The energy to change the state of one kilogram with no temperature change
The energy needed to raise one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius
The energy needed to change one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius

items.why: This is the definition: the energy required to change the state of one kilogram of the substance with no change in temperature.

items.stem: Which equation gives the energy needed for a change of state?

options.text: energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat × ∆θ
energy for a state change = mass ÷ specific latent heat
energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat
energy for a change of state = mass × specific heat capacity

items.why: This is the specification equation, written in symbols as E = m L.

items.stem: The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 330 000 J/kg. How much energy is needed to melt 0.30 kg of ice that is already at 0 °C?
In E = m L, which units does the specification give for the three quantities?

options.text: E in joules, m in kilograms, L in joules per kilogram
E in joules, m in kilograms, L in joules per kilogram per °C
E in joules, m in grams, L in joules per kilogram of substance
E in joules per second, m in kilograms, L in joules per kilogram

items.why: The specification gives energy, E, in joules, J; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; specific latent heat, L, in joules per kilogram, J/kg.

items.stem: Which change of state does the specific latent heat of fusion describe?

options.text: The change of state from liquid to vapour, that is boiling
The change of state from a solid straight to a vapour
The change of state from a solid to a liquid, that is melting
The change of state from liquid into a warmer liquid

items.why: The specification gives specific latent heat of fusion as the change of state from solid to liquid.

items.stem: Which change of state does the specific latent heat of vaporisation describe?

options.text: The change of state from a solid straight into a gas
The change of state from solid to liquid
The rise in temperature of the vapour formed
The change of state from a liquid to a vapour

items.why: The specification gives specific latent heat of vaporisation as the change of state from liquid to vapour.

items.stem: A solid is heated at a steady rate and a graph of temperature against time is plotted. What does a flat section of the graph show?

options.text: The substance is changing state while energy is supplied
The substance has reached the hottest temperature it can ever reach
The heater has been switched off, so no energy is transferred
The substance is warming too slowly for the thermometer

items.why: A flat section means constant temperature: the energy supplied is producing the change of state.

items.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes specific heat capacity from specific latent heat?

options.text: They are two names for one quantity, so either may be used for any change
Specific heat capacity needs a temperature change; latent heat does not
Specific heat capacity changes state; specific latent heat changes temperature
Either quantity may be used for any thermal change at all

items.why: c is the energy per kilogram per degree Celsius of temperature change; L is the energy per kilogram to change state at constant temperature.

items.stem: Which statement about the molecules of a gas is correct?

options.text: They are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is related to their average kinetic energy.
They are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is set by their total kinetic energy.
They all move at one single fixed speed, and the temperature of the gas is set by that shared speed.
They move along fixed repeating paths, and the temperature of the gas is set by their spacing.

items.why: This is what the specification states: the molecules of a gas are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

items.stem: A sealed container of gas is heated and the temperature of the gas rises. What happens to the molecules of the gas?

options.text: They all speed up by exactly the same amount and keep sharing one common speed.
Their average kinetic energy rises, so the molecules move faster on average.
Each molecule expands, so the gas now fills more of the container space.
They collide with one another less often, now that they have energy.

items.why: The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules, so raising the temperature raises that average and the molecules move faster on average.

items.stem: A fixed mass of gas is sealed in a rigid container, so its volume cannot change. The gas is then heated. What happens to the pressure the gas exerts?

options.text: It stays the same, because the trapped gas is not able to expand.
It falls, because the heated molecules swell and spread apart.
It increases, because the molecules hit the walls harder.
It rises briefly, then falls back to its old value.

items.why: Changing the temperature of a gas held at constant volume changes the pressure exerted: the faster molecules strike the walls more often and with greater force.

items.stem: What causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the walls of its container?

options.text: The gas molecules repelling each other and pushing on the walls.
The weight of the gas above pressing down on the container.
The molecules swelling up and pressing against the walls.
The molecules of the gas colliding with the walls of it.

items.why: Gas pressure comes from the huge number of collisions the randomly moving molecules make with the walls each second, each collision exerting a small force.

items.stem: Two identical rigid sealed flasks hold the same gas. Flask X is kept at 20 °C and flask Y at 80 °C. Why is the pressure in flask Y higher?

options.text: The molecules in Y have swollen to a larger size, so they press harder on the walls.
The molecules in Y have a greater average kinetic energy, so they hit the walls harder.
The molecules in Y repel one another far more strongly at the higher temperature.
The molecules in Y are packed more closely together than those in flask X.

items.why: The higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy, so in the same fixed volume the collisions with the walls are both more frequent and more forceful.

items.stem: A fixed mass of gas is cooled while its volume is kept constant. Using the particle model, what happens to the pressure of the gas?

options.text: It stays the same, because the rigid container will not let the gas shrink at all.
It increases, because the cooled molecules move closer to the walls of it.
It decreases, because slower molecules hit the walls less often and less hard.
It decreases, because the molecules shrink in size as the gas cools down.

items.why: Cooling lowers the average kinetic energy, so the molecules collide with the walls both less frequently and with less force, and the pressure falls.

items.stem: The pressure of a gas produces a net force on the wall of its container. In which direction does that net force act?

options.text: At an angle that depends on the shape of the container.
Along the surface of the wall, in the direction of flow.
Straight down, because of the weight of the gas.
At right angles to the surface of the container wall.

items.why: The specification states that the pressure produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container, or any surface, because the sideways parts of the impacts cancel.

items.stem: Which statement about a gas and changes of pressure is correct?

options.text: A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes.
A gas keeps a fixed volume whatever pressure is applied to it.
A gas can be expanded by pressure changes but never compressed.
A gas can only be compressed if it is squeezed from above.

items.why: This is the specification statement: the molecules of a gas are far apart, so a change of pressure can squeeze the gas into a smaller volume or let it expand.

items.stem: A fixed mass of gas is allowed to expand into a larger volume at constant temperature. Using the particle model, why does the pressure decrease?

options.text: Each molecule strikes the wall more gently, since it now has less kinetic energy.
The molecules cool down as they spread out into the much larger space.
The molecules travel further between wall collisions, so there are fewer collisions.
The molecules shrink in size once they are given more room to move about.

items.why: At constant temperature the molecules keep the same average speed, but in a larger volume each one takes longer to reach a wall, so the collision rate and the pressure both fall.

items.stem: Under which conditions does the relationship pressure × volume = constant apply to a gas?

options.text: Any mass of gas at all, whatever its temperature happens to be doing.
A fixed mass of gas whose temperature is steadily climbing.
Any gas at all, so long as its container has been sealed.
A fixed mass of gas that is being held at a constant temperature.

items.why: The specification introduces the relationship with exactly this condition: for a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature, pressure × volume = constant.

items.stem: For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature, which relationship does the specification give?

options.text: pressure × volume = constant, written as [p V = constant]
pressure ÷ volume = constant, written as [p / V = a constant]
pressure = volume × constant, written as [p = k V]
pressure × volume = temperature, written as [p V = T]

items.why: This is the relationship exactly as the specification states it, together with the symbol form the specification gives in brackets.

items.stem: Which units does the specification give for the two quantities in p V = constant?

options.text: Pressure in newtons, N, and volume in centimetres cubed, cm^3.
Pressure in pascals, Pa, and volume in metres cubed, m^3.
Pressure in pascals, Pa, and volume in cubic centimetres, cm^3.
Pressure in pascals, Pa, and volume in metres squared, m^2.

items.why: The specification states pressure, p, in pascals, Pa, and volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3.

items.stem: A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 0.125 m^3 at a pressure of 80 kPa. At constant temperature the pressure is increased to 800 kPa. What is the new volume of the gas?
items.why: p V = constant, so 80 × 0.125 = 800 × V, giving V = 10 ÷ 800 = 0.0125 m^3. The pressure is ten times larger, so the volume is ten times smaller.

items.stem: A fixed mass of gas at a pressure of 300 kPa occupies 0.020 m^3. At constant temperature it is allowed to expand to 0.150 m^3. What is the new pressure of the gas?

options.text: 40 kPa
300 kPa
2250 kPa

items.why: p V = constant, so 300 × 0.020 = p × 0.150, giving p = 6.0 ÷ 0.150 = 40 kPa. The gas has expanded, so the pressure must fall.

items.stem: In physics, what is meant by work?

options.text: Work is the energy stored inside a moving body.
Work is the transfer of energy by a force.
Work is a force acting over a given distance.
Work is the heating caused by a force.

items.why: This is the specification statement: work is the transfer of energy by a force.

items.stem: A cyclist uses a bicycle pump to inflate a tyre, and the barrel of the pump becomes noticeably warm. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Friction between the piston seal and the barrel is the only cause of the warming.
Warm air is drawn in from outside, and that air heats the metal barrel.
Work is done on the gas as it is compressed, raising its internal energy.
The gas loses internal energy as it is squeezed, so heat is released.

items.why: The piston exerts a force that moves, so work is done on the enclosed gas. That transfer increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause its temperature to rise.
